title: vlt 1.0 Ships as a Drop-in npm Replacement with Phased Installs, Graph Queries, and Malware-Blocking
gist: vlt, built by npm's original creators, shipped 1.0 as a drop-in npm-compatible package manager that splits install/execute into two phases (vlt install then vlt build) to stop lifecycle scripts running automatically, adds a 60+ selector dependency-graph query language, and has flagged over 275,000 malicious package versions at its hosted registry — a quarter of which the article notes are still installable on npm — though on raw install speed pnpm and Bun still lead even as vlt claims its registry is up to 38% faster than npm's.

themes.theme: Phased installs as the core security redesign

insights.claim: vlt splits npm's single-step download-extract-run-scripts process into two explicit commands: vlt install (downloads and extracts packages without executing anything) and vlt build (runs scripts only for trusted packages, skipping anything flagged as malware by default).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A structural, not just configurable, separation of download from execution closes the specific attack vector (auto-run postinstall scripts) exploited in most recent npm supply-chain attacks — a template other package managers may need to match.
insights.locator: Where npm downloads, extracts, and runs lifecycle scripts in one step paragraph

insights.claim: vlt founder Darcy Clarke describes the client as 'built so nothing runs on your machine just because you typed install,' framing phased installation as vlt's core design philosophy rather than an optional safety flag.
insights.speaker: Darcy Clarke
insights.so_what: Signals vlt's positioning is security-first by default architecture, not opt-in hardening — relevant for evaluating whether vlt can win developer trust faster than incumbents retrofitting safety features.
insights.quote: built so nothing runs on your machine just because you typed install

themes.theme: Graph query language as a differentiator

insights.claim: vlt query introduces a CSS-like selector syntax with more than 60 selectors for querying the dependency graph as if it were a DOM tree; roughly half of these selectors are security-focused and powered by a Socket integration, enabling at-scale dependency auditing, and a :host(local) selector extends queries across every project on a machine.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A DOM-like query interface for dependency graphs is a genuinely novel developer-ergonomics feature that could become a competitive wedge for security/audit tooling built on top of vlt's graph model.
insights.locator: The second standout is vlt query paragraph

insights.claim: vlt query supports a --view=mermaid flag that renders matched dependencies as a diagram, embedding visualization directly into the CLI dependency-audit workflow.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Built-in diagram export lowers the friction for teams to communicate dependency-risk findings (e.g., in security reviews or incident reports) without external tooling.
insights.locator: The second standout is vlt query paragraph

themes.theme: Competitive landscape: npm ecosystem's post-Shai-Hulud security race

insights.claim: Following a year of supply-chain attacks such as the Shai-Hulud worm, the whole npm ecosystem has been converging on script-blocking defaults: npm v12 now disables install scripts by default, pnpm quarantines fresh releases with a minimum release age, and Bun also blocks postinstall scripts.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Documents an industry-wide security-hardening trend across all major JS package managers triggered by a single named attack (Shai-Hulud) — a case study in how a supply-chain incident reshapes tooling defaults across an entire ecosystem within about a year.
insights.locator: After a year of supply chain attacks such as the Shai-Hulud worm paragraph

insights.claim: vlt differentiates from npm, pnpm, and Bun's script-blocking approaches by rejecting bad packages directly at the registry level, having flagged more than 275,000 malicious package versions — a quarter of which reviewers note are still installable on npm.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The claim that a quarter of vlt's 275,000+ flagged malicious versions remain installable on npm today is a concrete, checkable data point exposing a live security gap in npm's registry moderation relative to vlt's registry-level filtering.
insights.locator: vlt goes further by rejecting bad packages at the registry paragraph

insights.claim: On raw install speed, pnpm and Bun still lead the field; vlt instead claims its hosted registry is up to 38% faster than npm's, a narrower and different performance claim than 'fastest overall.'
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Investors/engineers should note vlt is not pitching itself as the fastest installer — its performance value proposition is registry-fetch speed relative to npm specifically, not a general performance win over pnpm/Bun.
insights.locator: On raw install speed, though, pnpm and Bun still lead paragraph

insights.claim: Migration to vlt is designed to be low-friction: after a global npm install -g vlt, teams run vlt install and vlt build in an existing project, with config moving from .npmrc to vlt.json and a new vlt-lock.json lockfile, and the npm-compatible registry API keeps existing CI pipelines, private registries, and tooling working.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Low migration friction (npm-API compatibility, familiar CLI verbs) reduces switching costs for enterprises evaluating vlt as an npm drop-in replacement, improving its realistic adoption odds versus a ground-up replacement.
insights.locator: For developers who are interested, migrating steps are small paragraph

insights.claim: vlt is free and open source under a BSD-2-Clause-Patent license, developed by vlt technology inc., while the company's hosted registries and ecosystem mirrors reached general availability alongside the 1.0 client release.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The open-source client plus hosted-registry model mirrors an open-core monetization strategy (free tooling, paid/hosted infrastructure) — relevant for assessing vlt technology inc.'s revenue path.
insights.locator: vlt is free and open source under a BSD-2-Clause-Patent license paragraph

insights.claim: Founder Darcy Clarke's own pitch to skeptical Hacker News commenters framed vlt's value as saving time and money, reducing supply-chain risk, and lowering infrastructure/CI costs via API performance and payload optimizations, specifically targeting teams paying high CI/agent bills where cold installs consume a large share of total build time.
insights.speaker: Darcy Clarke
insights.so_what: vlt's go-to-market pitch explicitly targets CI cost pain (slow cold installs inflating CI/agent bills) as the wedge for enterprise adoption, not just security — a dual value proposition worth testing against real customer CI cost data.
insights.quote: vlt helps engineering teams build JavaScript software faster, reduce supply chain risk, and lower infrastructure costs (via. API perf / payload optimizations).
insights.locator: On Hacker News, where the launch reached the front page paragraph
